[PREVIOUS WORK]
# Program *Bridge*
## End-of-Life and Migration Program for Platform L → Platform N

**Program envelope:** 60 months of active program (M−6 → M54), with residual bridge-component obligations extending to ~M78. Public customer-facing headline: *"Platform L is supported through M42; a limited, paid, plan-gated extension path exists to M54."*

> **Working assumptions — replace with your actuals.** All figures below labeled *(illustrative)* are placeholders whose purpose is to show the model structure and force the arithmetic to close. The decision logic holds regardless of the inputs.
>
> | Input | Assumption *(illustrative)* |
> |---|---|
> | Platform L revenue | $260M/yr; contribution profit $150M ≈ 33% of company profit |
> | Accounts on L | ~4,000, of which ~40 "Strategic" accounts = ~55% of L revenue |
> | Deployment mix | 45% vendor-hosted, 50% customer on-prem, 5% air-gapped/regulated |
> | OEM/embedded partners | 14 partners, ~6% of L revenue, ~900 downstream end-customers |
> | Sustaining cost | ~$28M/yr, growing 10–15%/yr |
> | Key-person exposure | 9 engineers hold sole ownership of L subsystems; 4 retire within 36 months |

---

# 1. Strategic options: why sunset, and what stays on the table

The board will ask why we are not simply keeping or selling L. The plan must show the comparison.

| Option | Description | NPV *(illustrative, 7-yr)* | Security liability | Customer relationship | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Sunset & migrate** (recommended) | Publish EOL, rebuild the load-bearing capabilities on N, fund migration | **+$310M** | Extinguished by M42/M54 | Preserved if executed well; ~8–12% churn expected | **Adopt** |
| **B. Divest / license L** to a specialist maintenance roll-up | Carve out code, contracts, and 2–3 sustaining engineers; buyer supports the tail | +$150M to +$240M (high variance) | **Transferred** — the single largest benefit | Relationship intermediated; N cross-sell rights must be contractually reserved | **Reject as the whole answer; retain as a live option for the residual tail (see §1.1)** |
| **C. Reprice and hold** — fund L via 2–3× maintenance uplift, no sunset | Keep L indefinitely, self-funded | −$40M to +$90M, degrading | **Retained and compounding** | Buys 24–36 months of peace, then a worse version of the same crisis with fewer engineers and a hostile installed base | **Reject** (documented as baseline) |

**Why A over C:** repricing does not buy engineers who no longer exist, and it does not remove the unpatchable-dependency risk. It converts an operational problem into an existential one on a delay.

**Why A over B outright:** B forfeits the ~85% of L revenue that is migratable to N, and a roll-up buyer's incentive is to harvest, not to keep our customers warm for N. Divesting the *whole* base sells our own future revenue at a discount.

### 1.1 The hybrid: reserve B for the residual

At the **M30 gate (G4)** we will know the size of the irreducible residue — accounts that cannot or will not migrate (air-gapped, regulated-frozen, acquired, contractually locked). Two paths:

- Residue **< ~2% of L revenue** → run Custom Support Agreements to M54 in-house.
- Residue **> ~2%** → execute a **carve-out transfer** of that segment (code branch + contracts + a small sustaining team) to a specialist provider, with a reserved right of re-approach for N. This is strictly better than running an in-house museum staffed by contractors.

**Action now:** run a quiet market-sounding of 3–4 maintenance roll-up buyers during Phase 0 so the option is priced, not theoretical, when G4 arrives.

---

# 2. Operating principles

1. **You cannot keep L.** The cost curve compounds, the knowledge base is evaporating, and unpatchable upstream dependencies convert a financial problem into an existential one. Time is not neutral; waiting is the expensive option.
2. **You cannot force-march the top accounts.** They are a third of the profit and they have credible alternatives. A migration experienced as coercion converts a support problem into a competitive loss.
3. **Job parity, not feature parity.** Rebuild the *outcomes* a handful of loyal customers depend on; be ruthless about the long tail of toggles nobody uses.
4. **Published dates; capped, priced, plan-gated exceptions; no free extensions.**
   *(This replaces the seductive but dishonest slogan "dates never slip." Our dates* can *move: earlier under the security tripwire (§4.4), later only via a paid, approval-gated, individually capped Custom Support Agreement that requires a signed migration completion date. We say this out loud on day one, because sophisticated procurement will work it out in the first hour and we would rather be trusted than clever.)*
5. **Commitments before deadlines.** We publish the parity commitments and the tooling roadmap *at the same moment* as the shutoff calendar — never the deadline first.
6. **Early is cheapest, and that never reverses.** Incentives decay on a published schedule and are never improved retroactively for latecomers (§7.4). The first time we hold this line under pressure is the moment the whole program becomes credible.

---

# 3. Phase 0 — Discovery, instrumentation, and readiness (M−6 → M0)

**Nothing is announced until Gate G0 passes.** An EOL date announced without usage data, a parity commitment, and a sustaining plan is how you lose your top ten accounts in one quarter.

| # | Workstream | Output | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Usage telemetry / fingerprinting | Per-account, per-feature, per-API usage map; ≥85% of L installs instrumented (on-prem: opt-in agent, log ingest, or funded audit) | Eng + Data |
| 2 | Feature census | Every capability, flag, endpoint, report, export format, connector — with active-user counts and revenue attachment | Product |
| 3 | **Dependency EOL calendar** (§4.5) | Every OS, DB, runtime, crypto library, browser, appliance, and third-party component mapped to *its own* vendor EOL date against M0–M54 | Platform Eng + Security |
| 4 | Account segmentation & defection risk model | Tier assignment (§7.1) + risk scores (§8.1) | Sales Ops + CS |
| 5 | Cost-of-carry model | True annual L cost incl. security, infra, insurance loading, and opportunity cost of engineers | Finance |
| 6 | **Key-person / knowledge asset audit** | Subsystems with fewer than two competent owners; retirement dates; sustaining plan inputs (§5) | Eng leadership |
| 7 | Legal review | Contract-by-contract: perpetual licenses, evergreen support commitments, notice periods, OEM/embedded rights, regulated obligations, MFN clauses, termination-for-convenience terms | Legal |
| 8 | Competitive intel & switching-cost model | Rival migration offers, poaching targets, realistic TCO of switching to a competitor | Product Marketing |
| 9 | Divest option sounding | Indicative pricing from 3–4 maintenance roll-ups (§1.1) | Corp Dev |
| 10 | Financial model & investor narrative | Profit bridge, guidance treatment (§6) | CFO + IR |

### 3.1 Cover narrative and leak plan

Six months of instrumentation, funded audits, and contract review across 4,000 accounts and a field organization **will leak.** Plan for it rather than pretending otherwise.

- **Honest public framing from M−6:** *"We are running a Platform Modernization Assessment across our product line to plan the next decade of investment."* This is true, non-deniable-later, and consistent with the eventual announcement.
- **Leak-response kit ready at M−6:** pre-drafted holding statement, field FAQ, and an accelerated Tier 1 briefing sequence that can be triggered within 48 hours. If a credible leak occurs, we **pull the announcement forward** rather than deny it. Denial is the one action that cannot be recovered from.
- **Field discipline:** no rep is briefed on the EOL decision before M−1. Reps are given a truthful, sufficient answer for the assessment framing. Anyone who speculates on dates is corrected in writing.
- **Gate G0 exit criteria (see §11.2)** include "leak-response kit tested" and "Tier 1 briefing calendar locked."

---

# 4. Sunset timeline and support policy

## 4.1 The single support & price ladder

One table. This supersedes any prior pricing statements and is published as a versioned policy document that becomes the contractual reference.

| State | Window | **Hosted L** | **On-prem L** | Price (× current effective maintenance) | Included | Excluded |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Full Support** | M0 → M18 | Yes | Yes | **1.0×** (price-locked for accounts on a signed migration plan) | Security patches, Sev-1→4 fixes, dependency compatibility certifications, migration-blocker fixes, full SLAs | New features (frozen M0) |
| **Maintenance Support** | M18 → M30 | Yes | Y

[NEW REQUEST]
An online retailer's return rate has climbed to 28% of shipped units, and processing returns now costs more per unit than the original outbound fulfillment. Returned goods pile up in a manual inspection queue, many are resold too late at deep discounts, and a growing share is simply scrapped. Customer research warns that tightening the return policy is the single fastest way to lose share to rivals.

Redesign the returns operation so it stops destroying margin without degrading the customer promise. Address return prevention, triage and grading, refurbishment and secondary channels, network design for reverse flows, and the data feedback loop to merchandising — and quantify how success should be measured.
[END ORIGINAL REQUEST]

# Critic Review

## 1. Blocking issue: there is no output to review

The previous step produced **nothing** for the new request. The only artifact carried forward is Program *Bridge* — a platform EOL/migration plan — which is (a) unrelated to the returns problem and (b) itself **truncated mid-table** at §4.1 (`| **Maintenance Support** | M18 → M30 | Yes | Y`). Two conclusions:

- Nothing can be assessed on merit; this cannot pass.
- The truncation is a warning about the likely failure mode of the next attempt: a sprawling, table-heavy document that runs out of room before reaching the parts the user explicitly asked for. The returns request has **six mandated topics plus quantification**. Front-load the economics and the measurement framework; do not spend the budget on a 40-row disposition matrix and die before the data loop.

## 2. What a passing answer must contain (gap list)

### 2.1 Unit economics baseline — mandatory, and it must close arithmetically
The user's central fact is that *return processing now costs more per unit than outbound fulfillment*. An answer that does not open with a reconciled per-unit cost stack has not engaged the problem. Required:

- Fully loaded reverse cost stack per returned unit: inbound return freight, receive/scan, queue dwell (carrying + value decay), inspect/grade labor, repack/re-poly, restock or transfer, refund payment processing, contact-center touch, plus **recovery loss** (markdown vs. original price) and **scrap write-off**.
- Compare directly against outbound cost/unit so the inversion is visible and quantified.
- A **recovery waterfall** on 100 returned units: % restocked A-grade at full price, % outlet, % refurb, % B2B liquidation, % donate/recycle, % scrap — each with net recovery as a share of original retail. Percentages must sum; recovery must reconcile to the aggregate margin bleed.
- Carry forward the prior artifact's one genuine strength: an explicit **"illustrative assumptions — replace with your actuals"** block (GMV, units, AOV, category mix, current 28% rate split by category and by reason). But do not let "illustrative" become an excuse to skip the arithmetic; at least one worked chain must close end to end.

### 2.2 Honor the binding constraint, explicitly
Research says tightening policy is the fastest way to lose share. The answer must therefore **define the customer promise as a measurable, frozen set of commitments** (returns window length, free return shipping threshold, refund latency, number of steps/ease) and then prove every intervention leaves those numbers equal or better. Interventions must be sorted into:

- **Friction-neutral or friction-reducing prevention** (allowed): size/fit guidance and per-SKU size-curve correction, richer PDP content (dimensions, on-model, fabric, video), review/Q&A mining, defect and mis-pick reduction, packaging changes, delivery-damage reduction, exchange-first and instant-exchange flows, returnless refunds below a cost threshold, instant refunds for good-standing customers.
- **Policy tightening** (prohibited by the brief): shorter windows, restocking fees, paid return shipping as a blanket change.
- **The hard middle: serial-return abuse.** Must be addressed, not dodged — but flagged as adjacent to prohibited tightening, with a segmented, evidence-based approach, a false-positive tolerance, and explicit legal/PR risk. Do not hand-wave this.

### 2.3 Triage and grading — the manual queue is the bottleneck; treat it as one
Weakness to avoid: describing a nicer inspection process without doing the throughput math.

- **Move the disposition decision upstream of physical inspection.** Predictive disposition from return reason + SKU + customer history + item value at initiation, so a share of units never enter the inspect queue at all (returnless refund, direct-to-liquidation cross-dock, direct-to-refurb-partner). State the target % dispositioned pre-receipt.
- Queue discipline: **not FIFO.** Order by value-at-risk × decay rate. WIP cap, takt time, units/hour/inspector, staffing model, and explicit **January/post-peak surge capacity** plan (seasonality is missing from most answers here).
- Grade taxonomy with objective, photographable criteria; inter-rater reliability target; audit sampling; first-pass grading accuracy as a tracked metric.
- **Value decay must be explicit** — a %/week decay curve by category (apparel vs. electronics vs. home differ sharply), driving dwell-time SLAs. "Resold too late at deep discounts" is a *speed* failure, not a channel failure; the answer must say so.

### 2.4 Refurbishment and secondary channels
- Grade → channel decision matrix scored on **net recovery after cost-to-serve**, not gross resale price. A channel with a higher headline price and a second touch can be worse.
- Make-vs-buy on refurb capability; warranty terms on refurbished units; parts harvesting for high-value SKUs.
- Cannibalization guardrails (outlet vs. full-price, MAP/brand-partner constraints, geographic/temporal separation).
- Donate (tax treatment) and recycle as economically modeled options, not moral afterthoughts.
- **Scrap must be attacked as a reputational as well as financial line item** — EU/France restrictions on destroying unsold goods and ESG scrutiny are live risks. The brief says scrap is *growing*; an answer that treats it as residual has missed a headline.

### 2.5 Reverse network design
Frequently the thinnest section. Must cover:
- Dedicated returns/processing nodes vs. returns into forward DCs (double-touch cost), hub-and-spoke vs. distributed, number and siting logic.
- Consolidation at drop-off partners / label-less returns / store returns if applicable, and the trade between customer convenience and consolidation density.
- **Sell/ship from the returns center** so A-grade and outlet units avoid a second inbound leg.
- Cross-dock lanes straight to liquidation/refurb partners.
- Cross-border returns: duty/VAT reclaim, in-market processing vs. repatriation.
- Carrier/mode mix and the cost of speed on the reverse leg (paying more for faster inbound can be NPV-positive when decay is steep — show this).

### 2.6 Data feedback loop to merchandising
- A **causal** reason-code taxonomy (mis-sized / mis-described / defective / damaged in transit / wrong item shipped / changed mind / bracketing), captured at variant level, with root-cause **ownership assigned** (vendor, listing team, DC, carrier, buyer).
- The decisive change: make **return-adjusted contribution margin** the merchandising KPI, replacing gross margin, at SKU/variant/vendor/category level. Without this, nothing upstream changes.
- Vendor scorecards, defect chargebacks, size-chart corrections, PDP fix workflow with an SLA, and explicit **delist / re-buy-quantity rules** — assortment surgery is a legitimate lever.
- Governance: who owns the number, what forum reviews it, what decision it is allowed to change. A dashboard with no decision rights is not a feedback loop.

### 2.7 Measurement — and anti-gaming
The single biggest trap: naming "reduce return rate" as the headline KPI. That directly incentivizes the one thing the brief forbids (covert policy tightening) and can be hit by shrinking the business. Required structure:

- **Economic metrics:** fully loaded cost per returned unit; net recovery rate (% of original retail); scrap rate; return-adjusted contribution margin.
- **Speed/flow:** dwell time receipt→disposition; % dispositioned pre-receipt; resale-within-N-days; queue WIP.
- **Quality:** first-pass grading accuracy; mis-pick and defect rates; return-reason mix shift.
- **Customer guardrails (veto metrics, not scorecard decoration):** refund latency, returner repeat-purchase rate, NPS/CSAT among returners, share/conversion in returns-sensitive segments. Any prevention initiative that moves a guardrail adversely is rolled back regardless of margin gain.
- Explicit statement that return rate is a **diagnostic, not a target**, plus a policy-change freeze so the program cannot be "won" by degrading the promise.
- A quantified target end state with a stated bridge: how much of today's bleed is addressable by prevention vs. speed vs. channel mix vs. processing cost, and the residual that is structurally irreducible.

### 2.8 Missing scaffolding
- **Sequencing:** 0–90 day quick wins (WIP cap, grade-at-receipt, returnless-refund threshold, top-50 SKU PDP/size fixes) that self-fund the capex items (automation, refurb line, network node) at 6–18 months.
- **Ownership/org:** returns is currently orphaned between ops and merchandising. Name a single owner with a returns P&L, or the data loop will not bite.
- **Risk register:** returnless-refund and fraud abuse rates, brand damage from used-goods resale, restocking-fee/withdrawal-right regulation, labor implications of inspection automation, dependency on reason-code capture quality.

## 3. Style guidance for the rewrite

Keep from Program *Bridge*: the assumptions table, the options-with-verdicts comparison, the "operating principles" that pre-commit to hard trade-offs, and stage gates. Drop from it: unexplained NPV precision, ladder tables so long they consume the document, and — critically — **finish the document.** If length is tight, compress the channel matrix and preserve the economics, the customer-promise guardrails, and the measurement section.

---

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**
[END QUALITY FEEDBACK]

- Fully loaded reverse cost stack per returned unit: inbound return freight, receive/scan, queue dwell (carrying + value decay), inspect/grade labor, repack/re-poly, restock or transfer, refund payment processing, contact-center touch, plus **recovery loss** (markdown vs. original price) and **scrap write-off**.
- Compare directly against outbound cost/unit so the inversion is visible and quantified.
- A **recovery waterfall** on 100 returned units: % restocked A-grade at full price, % outlet, % refurb, % B2B liquidation, % donate/recycle, % scrap — each with net recovery as a share of original retail. Percentages must sum; recovery must reconcile to the aggregate margin bleed.
- Carry forward the prior artifact's one genuine strength: an explicit **"illustrative assumptions — replace with your actuals"** block (GMV, units, AOV, category mix, current 28% rate split by category and by reason). But do not let "illustrative" become an excuse to skip the arithmetic; at least one worked chain must close end to end.

### 2.2 Honor the binding constraint, explicitly
Research says tightening policy is the fastest way to lose share. The answer must therefore **define the customer promise as a measurable, frozen set of commitments** (returns window length, free return shipping threshold, refund latency, number of steps/ease) and then prove every intervention leaves those numbers equal or better. Interventions must be sorted into:

- **Friction-neutral or friction-reducing prevention** (allowed): size/fit guidance and per-SKU size-curve correction, richer PDP content (dimensions, on-model, fabric, video), review/Q&A mining, defect and mis-pick reduction, packaging changes, delivery-damage reduction, exchange-first and instant-exchange flows, returnless refunds below a cost threshold, instant refunds for good-standing customers.
- **Policy tightening** (prohibited by the brief): shorter windows, restocking fees, paid return shipping as a blanket change.
- **The hard middle: serial-return abuse.** Must be addressed, not dodged — but flagged as adjacent to prohibited tightening, with a segmented, evidence-based approach, a false-positive tolerance, and explicit legal/PR risk. Do not hand-wave this.

### 2.3 Triage and grading — the manual queue is the bottleneck; treat it as one
Weakness to avoid: describing a nicer inspection process without doing the throughput math.

- **Move the disposition decision upstream of physical inspection.** Predictive disposition from return reason + SKU + customer history + item value at initiation, so a share of units never enter the inspect queue at all (returnless refund, direct-to-liquidation cross-dock, direct-to-refurb-partner). State the target % dispositioned pre-receipt.
- Queue discipline: **not FIFO.** Order by value-at-risk × decay rate. WIP cap, takt time, units/hour/inspector, staffing model, and explicit **January/post-peak surge capacity** plan (seasonality is missing from most answers here).
- Grade taxonomy with objective, photographable criteria; inter-rater reliability target; audit sampling; first-pass grading accuracy as a tracked metric.
- **Value decay must be explicit** — a %/week decay curve by category (apparel vs. electronics vs. home differ sharply), driving dwell-time SLAs. "Resold too late at deep discounts" is a *speed* failure, not a channel failure; the answer must say so.

### 2.4 Refurbishment and secondary channels
- Grade → channel decision matrix scored on **net recovery after cost-to-serve**, not gross resale price. A channel with a higher headline price and a second touch can be worse.
- Make-vs-buy on refurb capability; warranty terms on refurbished units; parts harvesting for high-value SKUs.
- Cannibalization guardrails (outlet vs. full-price, MAP/brand-partner constraints, geographic/temporal separation).
- Donate (tax treatment) and recycle as economically modeled options, not moral afterthoughts.
- **Scrap must be attacked as a reputational as well as financial line item** — EU/France restrictions on destroying unsold goods and ESG scrutiny are live risks. The brief says scrap is *growing*; an answer that treats it as residual has missed a headline.

### 2.5 Reverse network design
Frequently the thinnest section. Must cover:
- Dedicated returns/processing nodes vs. returns into forward DCs (double-touch cost), hub-and-spoke vs. distributed, number and siting logic.
- Consolidation at drop-off partners / label-less returns / store returns if applicable, and the trade between customer convenience and consolidation density.
- **Sell/ship from the returns center** so A-grade and outlet units avoid a second inbound leg.
- Cross-dock lanes straight to liquidation/refurb partners.
- Cross-border returns: duty/VAT reclaim, in-market processing vs. repatriation.
- Carrier/mode mix and the cost of speed on the reverse leg (paying more for faster inbound can be NPV-positive when decay is steep — show this).

### 2.6 Data feedback loop to merchandising
- A **causal** reason-code taxonomy (mis-sized / mis-described / defective / damaged in transit / wrong item shipped / changed mind / bracketing), captured at variant level, with root-cause **ownership assigned** (vendor, listing team, DC, carrier, buyer).
- The decisive change: make **return-adjusted contribution margin** the merchandising KPI, replacing gross margin, at SKU/variant/vendor/category level. Without this, nothing upstream changes.
- Vendor scorecards, defect chargebacks, size-chart corrections, PDP fix workflow with an SLA, and explicit **delist / re-buy-quantity rules** — assortment surgery is a legitimate lever.
- Governance: who owns the number, what forum reviews it, what decision it is allowed to change. A dashboard with no decision rights is not a feedback loop.

### 2.7 Measurement — and anti-gaming
The single biggest trap: naming "reduce return rate" as the headline KPI. That directly incentivizes the one thing the brief forbids (covert policy tightening) and can be hit by shrinking the business. Required structure:

- **Economic metrics:** fully loaded cost per returned unit; net recovery rate (% of original retail); scrap rate; return-adjusted contribution margin.
- **Speed/flow:** dwell time receipt→disposition; % dispositioned pre-receipt; resale-within-N-days; queue WIP.
- **Quality:** first-pass grading accuracy; mis-pick and defect rates; return-reason mix shift.
- **Customer guardrails (veto metrics, not scorecard decoration):** refund latency, returner repeat-purchase rate, NPS/CSAT among returners, share/conversion in returns-sensitive segments. Any prevention initiative that moves a guardrail adversely is rolled back regardless of margin gain.
- Explicit statement that return rate is a **diagnostic, not a target**, plus a policy-change freeze so the program cannot be "won" by degrading the promise.
- A quantified target end state with a stated bridge: how much of today's bleed is addressable by prevention vs. speed vs. channel mix vs. processing cost, and the residual that is structurally irreducible.

### 2.8 Missing scaffolding
- **Sequencing:** 0–90 day quick wins (WIP cap, grade-at-receipt, returnless-refund threshold, top-50 SKU PDP/size fixes) that self-fund the capex items (automation, refurb line, network node) at 6–18 months.
- **Ownership/org:** returns is currently orphaned between ops and merchandising. Name a single owner with a returns P&L, or the data loop will not bite.
- **Risk register:** returnless-refund and fraud abuse rates, brand damage from used-goods resale, restocking-fee/withdrawal-right regulation, labor implications of inspection automation, dependency on reason-code capture quality.

## 3. Style guidance for the rewrite

Keep from Program *Bridge*: the assumptions table, the options-with-verdicts comparison, the "operating principles" that pre-commit to hard trade-offs, and stage gates. Drop from it: unexplained NPV precision, ladder tables so long they consume the document, and — critically — **finish the document.** If length is tight, compress the channel matrix and preserve the economics, the customer-promise guardrails, and the measurement section.

---

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**
